title: Sorting: Quick Sort Partition
oneLiner: The core move behind quicksort: pick a pivot, then rearrange so everything smaller ends up left of it and everything bigger ends up right.
keyTakeaway: Partitioning drops the pivot into its FINAL sorted position in one pass, with everything smaller to its left and everything bigger to its right -- recursively partitioning each side (that's quicksort) sorts the whole array without ever allocating a second array. That's why quicksort usually beats merge sort in practice despite sharing the same O(n log n) average case: no extra O(n) space for a merge step.
explanation: This uses the Lomuto partition scheme: pick the LAST element as the pivot. Keep a boundary index i marking the end of the "confirmed smaller than pivot" region, starting one before the array (i = -1, nothing confirmed yet). Walk a second pointer j across everything except the pivot itself: whenever nums[j] <= pivot, the boundary grows -- increment i, then swap nums[i] and nums[j] to pull that small value into the confirmed region. Once j has scanned everything, the pivot itself still needs to move: swap it from the end into position i + 1, which is now exactly where it belongs. Watch out for that last swap specifically -- it's easy to write the scan correctly and then forget the algorithm isn't done until the pivot itself actually moves into its final spot.

starterCode.python:
def partition(nums):
    # TODO: pivot = nums[-1]. i starts at -1 (boundary of the "smaller" region).
    # For j from 0 to second-to-last: if nums[j] <= pivot, i += 1 and swap nums[i], nums[j].
    # Finally swap nums[i + 1] and nums[-1] to drop the pivot into place.
    return nums

visualizationSteps.message: Starting array: [3, 6, 2, 8, 4]. Pivot = last element = 4. Boundary i = -1 (nothing confirmed smaller yet).
nums[0]=3 <= pivot (4) -- grow the boundary: i becomes 0, then swap nums[0] and nums[0].
nums[1]=6 > pivot (4) -- leave it, it already belongs in the "bigger" region.
nums[2]=2 <= pivot (4) -- grow the boundary: i becomes 1, then swap nums[1] and nums[2].
nums[3]=8 > pivot (4) -- leave it, it already belongs in the "bigger" region.
Scan done -- drop the pivot into place: swap nums[2] and the last index -> [3, 2, 4, 8, 6]. Pivot 4 is now at its final sorted index (2): everything left is <= it, everything right is bigger.

complexity.note: A single partition pass compares each element to the pivot once and swaps in place. (Full quicksort repeats this on sub-ranges: O(n log n) average.)
